newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal says referendum key to W.Sahara progress.
newsitem.headline: Portugal says referendum key to W.Sahara progress.

text.p: Portugal said progress on agreeing terms for a referendum on the disputed Western Sahara was needed for a breakthrough in talks which began in Lisbon on Monday between Morocco and its Polisario foes.

The two sides, who fought a 16-year war over the vast, mineral-rich territory, were meeting for the first time in the presence of United Nations mediators, led by former U.S. secretary of state James Baker.

Asked to outline the best possible result of the talks, Portuguese Foreign Minister Jaime Gama told reporters: "The process has been caught in an impasse over the organisation of the referendum and the electoral roll.
"If there were any agreement to make progress in this area, that would be important for the process and for such a complicated issue to reach a satisfactory solution."

The United Nations successfully brokered a ceasefire in 1991 but has since failed to implement a proposed referendum on the future of the 250,000 square km (100,000 sq mile) territory because Morocco and the Algeria-backed Polisario cannot agree on who should be allowed to vote.

The Polisario Front, which wants an independent state, has been holding out for only those resident in the territory before the Spanish colonial rulers left in 1976 to be allowed to take part in the ballot.
Morocco, which claims the territory as its own, wants the voting extended to tens of thousands of people who have moved there since.

Baker met Moroccan Prime Minister Abdellatif Filali and Mahfoud Ali Beiba, his counterpart in Polisario's self-proclaimed republic in Western Sahara, at a fortress near Lisbon on Monday. The officials made no comments before the three-day talks began.
Algerian Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf declined to speak to reporters after meeting Gama later in the foreign ministry.
The talks on the future of the Western Sahara, attended by representatives of Algeria and Mauritius, were being held behind closed doors and Baker was expected to make a final statement on Wednesday.

Baker, asked by U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan last March to spearhead a new bid to resolve the dispute, held separate talks with Moroccan and Polisario envoys in London earlier this month to set up the Lisbon meeting.

Morocco, which controls four-fifths of the territory with its potassium mines and rich Atlantic fishing grounds, hosted a meeting with the Polisario in Rabat last September, but U.N. officials were not present.
The talks made no significant progress.
But Baker said in London that both sides were showing new signs of flexibility on the question of the referendum.
